Start directly in the project library or on a blank canvas, following your preference.

The Chinese Liuye tool is Lasso fill in English, building color masses from closed shapes.
Draw a closed outline and release to fill it—ideal for petals and silhouettes.
The leaf-shaped tip follows the stroke, changing its width and pose as it turns.
Willow helps taper strokes and form leaves; it is separate from Lasso fill.

For repeating forms, enable symmetry and place the axis before painting.

Save chosen colors to a personal palette so painting stays decisive.
Pick colors already used on the canvas, or extract a related set of dominant hues.
Palettes support common exchange formats; check whether names survive export.
Gradients start with two color endpoints; linear and radial shapes suggest different space.
Fill lays regional color. Preview a gradient's reversal before committing.
A selection defines the editing area; a freehand lasso suits irregular shapes.
Rectangles and ellipses are regular; the wand finds areas by color.
Add or subtract selections, invert them, and refine edges to define the edit accurately.
Copy and cut move a region into a new layer, making revisions easier.
An indexed-color document keeps the whole pixel artwork within one palette.
It has its own tool limits; choose it to suit the artwork.
Separate the background and flowers into named layers, then gradually add local detail.
Reorder thumbnails and use groups to organize a more complex piece.
Preview and compare layer opacity and eight blending modes on the original canvas.
Alpha lock recolors existing shapes; content lock protects the layer.
Masks control layer visibility in black and white, preserving the original artwork.
Clipping confines new color to a base layer and helps preserve petal edges.
Preview a layer's position and size, then commit the transform as one complete edit.
Curves and gradient maps can be adjustment layers, leaving room to revise.
Basic vectors offer node editing; perspective assistants and comic lines can be previewed.
Before exporting complex layers, check which effects need baking.
Open the timeline to begin frame animation while keeping the familiar painting canvas.
Add a few simple changes and watch a form move from one frame to the next.
Duplicate a frame before changing it to preserve the established outline and color masses.
Onion skin helps compare neighboring positions without appearing in the output.
Timeline layer tracks reflect the artwork's structure; keyframes mark new content.
Held cells can share artwork; drag the ruler to browse a longer sequence.
Each frame's duration shapes the rhythm; check its emphasis and pauses in actual playback.
Adjust the range and direction; even a small animation benefits from clear timing.
Export a GIF or image atlas according to how the sequence will be shown and used.
GIF has color and alpha limits, and interchange formats do not preserve every feature.
This is an accelerated brush study, with colors sampled from the reference.
The reference is not imported as artwork; native brush marks build five stages.
Stage one lays in broad masses with a large Oils preset.
Separate bouquet and background, using black wrapping to support the red blooms.
Stage two establishes the main shadows and lit planes.
Read the large value relationships before describing individual petals.
Observe alternating cool and warm reds to separate the flower masses.
This sampled-color study shows marks accumulating, not real-time manual footage.
Stage three uses smaller marks to recover turns in foliage and wrapping.
Oil and Dry brush brushes leave different edges to distinguish the forms.
The impasto impression comes from arranged masses and directional marks.
This is not a three-dimensional paint simulation; values and edges do the work.
Stage four refines petals, reserving detail for the main roses.
Keep shadows simple; a few clear lit planes can describe the petals.
Compare this stage with the block-in before deciding how much to resolve.
Leave some edges unresolved so the painting retains quiet passages.
The last stage adds pale flowers and highlights, then checks the overall hierarchy.
The study canvas consists of real brush marks and is shown separately from the reference.
These are actual project-source excerpts explaining the work behind the interface.
A light editor-style layout makes the key code and responsibilities easier to read.
Compose Multiplatform is a declarative UI framework for Kotlin.
State defines the UI, buttons receive input, and the Rust engine handles pixels.
The pen pointer loads an image resource and sizes it from the base display density.
It connects to the system pointer service without adding a ring to the artwork.
Canvas input enters the coordination layer, with pen and touch sharing editing boundaries.
The input queue is bounded, and background work returns results to the display layer.
The Rust engine processes strokes and pixels, including closed-shape fills.
These canvas results come from the real engine, not a prerecorded effect animation.
The canvas is organized into tiles, so changed areas can be sent to the interface.
Shared unchanged pixels avoid repeated copying and retain earlier content for every undo.
History and project files also belong to the engine; the UI coordinates user actions.
Rust handles that work in the background; it is not all GPU computation.
Basic vectors and drawing assistants use the same path from parameters to previews.
Separating state from pixel work makes edits easier to preview and commit.
Desktop and mobile platforms have dedicated build targets.
Check the release page for downloads; devices and drivers still need validation.
Keep a project for editing and an image for sharing.
For layered effects and file exchange, check each format’s supported scope first.
